summary: The team arrives at Stanton Mick's subsurface facility on Luna to neutralize PSI activity. However, Mick reveals himself as a humanoid bomb and explodes, killing Runciter. The survivors barely escape with Runciter in cold-pac, retreating to their ship. During the chaotic evacuation, Joe realizes Pat Conley's extraordinary ability to alter the past was not used to save Runciter, though she claims it's too late. The chapter establishes the core mystery: whether they're genuinely dead or under attack by an external force.

narrative_significance: This chapter kills the novel's apparent protagonist and establishes the central ambiguity: are they in half-life after death, or are they still alive and under a devastating attack? The bomb's success raises questions about the reliability of Runciter's organization and introduces the possibility that the entire operation was compromised from the start. Pat Conley's character emerges as pivotal but enigmatic.

summary: The team flies back to Earth and takes Runciter to the Beloved Brethren Moratorium in Zurich, Switzerland. Joe encounters strange anomalies: his phone book is two years outdated, coins become obsolete, cream spoils, and his cigarette crumbles. While waiting for Runciter to be revived in half-life, Joe realizes the moratorium cannot establish contact with Runciter's consciousness. He travels to a hotel in Zurich and discovers that a woman—implied to be Wendy Wright—has deteriorated into a mummified corpse in the closet. The chapter shifts the mystery from external sabotage to internal deterioration.

narrative_significance: This chapter shifts the narrative focus from external conspiracy to internal metaphysical breakdown. Wendy's death suggests that something worse than the bomb attack is occurring: the survivors' own realities are decomposing. The chapter introduces the novel's central problem: not murder, but ontological decay. The discovery of Runciter's voice on the phone raises the question of whether he's truly dead or reaching out from half-life.

summary: Joe wakes in his Zurich hotel room to find Runciter's voice on his phone, seemingly in broadcast rather than interactive form. He attempts to use the phone but cannot reach the moratorium or order room service. A homeopape machine provides news of Runciter's death and funeral in Des Moines. The Ubik commercial appears on television with Runciter himself explaining that they're in half-life, that decay is natural, and that Ubik can help. Joe struggles to reconcile the scientific explanation with his surreal experience. He later encounters graffiti in a men's room stating 'I AM ALIVE. YOU'RE ALL DEAD.', written in Runciter's handwriting.

narrative_significance: This chapter's turning point is the revelation that they are dead and in half-life, confirmed by Runciter's TV commercial but complicated by the graffiti suggesting something more sinister. The Ubik product is introduced as a solution to half-life decay, yet it appears to be unavailable or unreliable. The commercial's contradictions—claiming to be pre-recorded while seeming to respond to Joe's thoughts—suggest that Runciter's presence may be more than mere recording technology. The chapter establishes that they are experiencing a collective phenomenon, not individual hallucinations.

ubik_slogan: My hair is so dry, so unmanageable. What's a girl to do? Simply rub in creamy Ubik hair conditioner. In just five days you'll discover new body in your hair, new glossiness. And Ubik hairspray, used as directed, is absolutely safe.
summary: Joe and Al travel to Baltimore to test their Runciter money at a random supermarket. They discover that Runciter currency is accepted but that all products—cigarettes, food, tape recorders—have mysteriously aged decades beyond their purchase dates. A carton of cigarettes contains a note from Runciter telling them not to give up. They return to New York where they find the elevator has regressed to an old iron cage, and Al begins to show signs of the same deterioration that killed Wendy. Graffiti in the men's room reveals the truth: they are dead and in half-life. Al separates from the group and appears to be dying.

Al's deterioration demonstrates that isolation from the group hastens death. The chapter pivots the narrative from mystery to horror as the characters confront their actual condition.

chapter_title: The Ubik Commercial and the Revelation of Reality
ubik_slogan: Has perspiration odor taken you out of the swim? Ten-day Ubik deodorant spray or Ubik roll-on ends worry of offending, brings you back where the happening is. Safe when used as directed in a conscientious program of body hygiene.
summary: Joe's apartment has regressed to 1939-era fixtures: wood stove, Victrola, pre-World War II furniture. A television broadcast shows Runciter's funeral in Des Moines, but then the TV switches on by itself and plays a Ubik commercial featuring Runciter, who explains that the decay is normal to half-life and that Ubik can reverse it. Joe receives a free sample by mail—but it's a jar of liver and kidney balm from 1908, not a spray can. Joe drives a 1939 LaSalle to an airfield, charters a Curtiss-Wright biplane, and trades the mysterious elixir bottle (which contains gold flakes) for passage to Des Moines. The chapter establishes that Joe is physically regressing through time, and that the world he inhabits is actively devolving.

narrative_significance: This chapter reveals that the regression is not random but directional—backward through the twentieth century toward the past. The Ubik product itself devolves as Joe tries to use it, suggesting that forces within the half-life environment are actively preventing access to the solution that Runciter promoted. The discovery that 1939 is a stable point in the regression (the date holds constant) suggests that there may be a limit to how far back the deterioration can go. Joe's ability to function in this regressed world despite his discomfort demonstrates human adaptability and persistence. The chapter sets up the final confrontation in Des Moines.

ubik_slogan: Taken as directed, Ubik provides uninterrupted sleep without morning-after grogginess. You awaken fresh, ready to tackle all those little annoying problems facing you. Do not exceed recommended dosage.
summary: Joe arrives in Des Moines and joins the surviving inertials at the Simple Shepherd Mortuary where Runciter's corpse lies in state—itself dehydrated and ancient-looking. The mortician, Mr. Bliss, drives Joe through 1939 Des Moines, and Joe experiences the era's racism and isolationism with revulsion. Joe learns that Edie Dorn has gone missing and is presumed dead from the same deterioration that killed Wendy and Al. The group realizes that separation hastens death. Runciter's body in the casket is found to be completely desiccated, having undergone the same decay as the other victims. Joe and the others understand they must stay together and reach Des Moines to reunite. The chapter explores how profoundly alienated they are from the past's moral and intellectual framework.

narrative_significance: This chapter marks the convergence of the surviving characters and the beginning of their collective confrontation with both the past and their own condition. The discovery that Runciter's body shows the same deterioration as the other victims complicates the narrative: if Runciter is supposedly alive and communicating from outside, why is his body in this state? The chapter suggests that the normal flow of time has been disrupted and that those who attempt to communicate across the temporal barrier (like Runciter) do so at great cost. The group's reunion provides both comfort and clarity as they begin to suspect forces beyond Pat Conley at work.

summary: Joe and the group search for a missing Edie Dorn who has begun deteriorating. A police citation appears with a handwritten warning from Runciter and directions to Archer's Drugstore. Joe discovers the drugstore oscillates between being a boarded-up 1939 ruin and a modern 1992 home-art store. Inside, he encounters the building pulsing between two states of reality. The manifestation suggests that reality itself is unstable and that there are at least two competing states trying to occupy the same physical space. The chapter demonstrates that the team's perception is beginning to diverge: different people see different realities. This divergence of perception preceded Wendy Wright's death, suggesting it is a harbinger of terminal deterioration.

narrative_significance: This chapter introduces the concept that reality is unstable not just through temporal regression, but through the superposition of multiple ontological states. The oscillating drugstore suggests that two realities—1939 and 1992—are attempting to occupy the same space simultaneously, creating a kind of ontological interference pattern. This foreshadows the revelation that they are in half-life, where consciousness exists in a liminal state between the world of the living and some form of afterlife. The breakdown of shared perception among the group members suggests that they are becoming isolated within their individual consciousness-realities, hastening their deterioration. The chapter demonstrates that external forces are actively manipulating their environment through infrastructure and commercial institutions.

chapter_title: The Ascent and the Encounter with Jory
ubik_slogan: Lift your arms and be all at once curvier! New extra-gentle Ubik bra and longline Ubik special bra means, Lift your arms and be all at once curvier! Supplies firm, relaxing support to bosom all day long when fitted as directed.
summary: Joe begins to deteriorate rapidly while ascending the stairs to his hotel room at the Meremont Hotel. His body weakens, his heart labors, and his clothes deteriorate into tatters. Pat Conley follows him, tormenting him with information about the nature of his condition and her knowledge of his attraction to Wendy Wright. Joe struggles up the stairs in an agonizing effort, finally reaching his room. As he enters, Glen Runciter appears and sprays him with a can of Ubik, saving his life. Runciter explains that they are in cold-pac at the Beloved Brethren Moratorium in Zurich, that they have been there for a week, and that the deterioration is due to both normal half-life decay and an external attack. Joe realizes that Runciter has been trying to reach them from the outside world. The chapter reaches an emotional climax as Joe is literally saved from death by Ubik.

narrative_significance: This chapter is the emotional center of the novel, where Joe experiences something like death-in-life and is rescued by external intervention. The appearance of Runciter in the hotel room raises the crucial question: if Runciter is outside in the real world, how is he physically present in the half-life world? This paradox suggests that Runciter's statement about being outside may itself be a deception or that the boundary between the worlds is more porous than anyone realizes. Ubik is revealed not as a commercial product but as a genuine metaphysical substance that can reverse the decay of half-life. The chapter demonstrates that salvation in this world comes not through individual effort but through the intervention of forces beyond one's control.

chapter_title: The Conversation and the Mystery Deepens
ubik_slogan: It takes more than a bag to seal in food flavor; it takes Ubik plastic wrap - actually four layers in one. Keeps freshness in, air and moisture out. Watch this simulated test.
summary: Runciter explains to Joe that they are indeed in cold-pac, that they have been interwired as a group to maintain collective consciousness, and that an external force is attacking them that is neither Pat Conley nor Ray Hollis. Runciter admits he doesn't know what is attacking them or where Ubik comes from. He reveals that Sammy Mundo is alive but in an irreversible coma, isolated from the group, and suggests that Mundo might be the attacker. Joe challenges Runciter's claims, pointing out inconsistencies and asking difficult questions. Runciter becomes defensive and emotional, admitting his uncertainty and powerlessness. The conversation establishes that even the supposedly alive Runciter doesn't fully understand their situation. The chapter questions the reliability of all information and the coherence of the reality they inhabit.

narrative_significance: This chapter dismantles the reliability of even the closest authority figure and suggests that all explanations may be incomplete or false. Runciter's uncertainty mirrors the readers' own confusion, establishing an epistemological principle: in this world, no one can be certain of the truth. The revelation about Sammy Mundo introduces an alternative theory of the attack—not external, but from within the group's own network. Mundo's isolation and comatose state suggest that consciousness itself might be the attacking force, that there could be a malevolent intelligence emerging from the combined unconsciousness of the group. The chapter establishes that the novel's fundamental mystery may be irresolvable through rational investigation alone.

chapter_title: The Spray and the Discovery of Jory
ubik_slogan: Could it be that I have bad breath, Tom? Well, Ed, if you're worried about that, try today's new Ubik, with powerful germicidal foaming action, guaranteed safe when taken as directed.
summary: Don Denny arrives at Joe's room with a doctor who finds Joe recovering well. When Denny uses the remaining Ubik spray, he is revealed to be Jory—a grotesquely malformed adolescent who has been consuming the life-force of the group members throughout their half-life. Jory explains that he has 'eaten' Wendy Wright, Don Denny, and others, and that he maintains the pseudo-world of 1939 Des Moines as a stage for his predation. He reveals that the regression was partially his doing but also partly natural decay, and that maintaining the environment exhausts him, forcing him to consume more half-lifers. Joe attacks Jory but is protected by the remaining Ubik. Joe leaves the room to explore and discovers that the world Jory has created is limited in scope—only a few blocks of Des Moines, with details degrading at the boundaries. The chapter reveals the true antagonist and nature of the threat.

narrative_significance: The revelation of Jory as the true antagonist transforms the novel from a mystery about external sabotage into a horror story about internal corruption. Jory represents a kind of consciousness that exists in half-life itself—not dead, not alive, but parasitic on the life-force of those frozen in cold-pac. His deformity and immaturity suggest that he is a broken or inverted consciousness, perhaps the result of brain damage or a fundamentally alien form of being. The chapter suggests that half-life is not simply an intermediate state but an environment populated by entities that feed on the preserved consciousness of the frozen. Jory's construction of the 1939 world and his maintenance of it through effort suggests a perverse mirror of the divine: a malevolent being creating and sustaining a pseudo-world for its own purposes. The chapter establishes that salvation requires not only external rescue (Ubik) but also a form of active resistance and struggle against the predatory forces within the half-life environment.

chapter_title: The Descent and the Encounter with Ella
ubik_slogan: Wake up to a hearty, lip-smacking bowlful of nutritious, nourishing Ubik toasted flakes, the adult cereal that's more crunchy, more tasty, more yummmish. Ubik breakfast cereal, the whole-bowl taste treat! Do not exceed recommended portion at any one meal.
summary: Joe explores the limitations of Jory's constructed world and realizes that it extends only a few blocks. He encounters a blond girl who reveals herself to be Ella Runciter, Glen's wife, who is in half-life but able to operate autonomously against Jory. Ella explains that she is deteriorating and will soon be reborn, and that she has been helping Joe because she wants him to become Glen's advisor in half-life after her departure. She gives Joe a certificate guaranteeing him a lifetime supply of Ubik. Ella and Joe go to a drugstore, but Jory has regressed the Ubik there into a nineteenth-century liver balm. Joe, with great effort, attempts to consciously evolve the balm back to a spray can, and a factory representative appears with the needed Ubik. The chapter establishes that there are forces within half-life working to counteract Jory, and that human will and consciousness can actually reshape the pseudo-world.

narrative_significance: This chapter introduces an entirely new dynamic: that there are benevolent forces within half-life working against Jory, and that these forces include those still conscious enough to act. Ella's revelation suggests that half-life is not simply a state of passive preservation but an environment where consciousness, will, and effort can produce material effects. The appearance of the factory representative summoned through Joe's concentrated will suggests that the world of the living and the world of half-life are more intimately connected than previously understood. The chapter emphasizes that salvation is not passive reception but active cooperation with forces of good. Joe's role as Ella's successor suggests that he will become a kind of guardian or healer within the half-life environment, using Ubik to combat Jory's predation. The chapter moves from horror to hope while maintaining ambiguity about the ultimate nature of the conflict and the identity of the forces involved.

chapter_title: The Closing Vision and the Eternal Return
ubik_slogan: I am Ubik. Before the universe was, I am. I made the suns. I made the worlds. I created the lives and the places they inhabit; I move them here, I put them there. They go as I say, they do as I tell them. I am the word and my name is never spoken, the name which no one knows. I am called Ubik, but that is not my name. I am. I shall always be.
summary: Glen Runciter waits at the moratorium to speak with Ella again. He discovers that his change-maker coins now bear Joe Chip's profile. The revelation suggests that as Ella departs the half-life world, Joe Chip is ascending in her place, his consciousness and influence permeating the system that maintains half-life. The final Ubik slogan reframes the product as a metaphysical principle—not merely a spray but a fundamental force of being that predates and transcends the universe. The novel ends with this ambiguous cosmological statement, suggesting that Ubik (or whatever principle it represents) is the ground of existence itself. The epilogue about Runciter discovering Joe's face on currency suggests the cyclical nature of the struggle and the possibility of eternal return and transformation within the half-life realm.

narrative_significance: The final chapter recontextualizes the entire narrative as not a rescue story but a transformation of the cosmic order. The appearance of Joe's face on currency suggests that consciousness, identity, and influence can be transferred across the boundary between life and half-life, and that those who persist in half-life may actually ascend to a higher status or role. The Ubik slogan transforms the commercial product into a theological and metaphysical statement: Ubik is not a manufactured item but a principle of being that predates creation and sustains all existence. The ending refuses narrative closure, instead opening onto an eternal mystery that encompasses all of reality. The novel suggests that the struggle with Jory is not a one-time event but an eternal recurrence—that new guardians will continually emerge to combat predatory forces, and that those who successfully resist become the protectors for the next iteration. The final image of Runciter discovering Joe's face on money suggests that Joe, through his struggle and spiritual growth, has become integrated into the fundamental fabric of their reality, hinting at apotheosis or divinization through suffering and persistence.
